title: Persian grammar
about: From your very first conversation to everyday fluency, one short lesson at a time. Each lesson gives you something you can say straight away, then the grammar that makes it work. You don't need to know any grammar: each grammar word is explained when you first need it. Every example is standard Iranian Persian, the Persian that is written and read aloud, with a reading in Latin letters that shows the vowels Persian doesn't write: â as in “father”, a as in “cat”, e as in “bed”, o as in “go”, i as in “see”, u as in “food”; kh and gh are said in the throat, ' is a catch in the voice, and a hyphen marks the small gap inside a Persian word and the ezafe, the little -e that joins words.

lessons.title: Say hello and who you are
lessons.summary: Greet someone, say your name and where you're from, and ask them the same: your first Persian conversation.
lessons.topic: {{من}} “I”, {{تو}} and {{شما}} “you”; {{هستم}}, {{هستی}}, {{هستید}} “am, are”; the verb at the end

goal.t: سلام، من سارا هستم. اهل کانادا هستم.
goal.r: salâm, man sârâ hastam. ahl-e kânâdâ hastam.
goal.tr: Hello, I'm Sara. I'm from Canada.

blocks.p: **The verb comes last.** Look at where {{هستم|hastam}} “am” goes: at the very end. {{من سارا هستم.|man sârâ hastam.}} is, word for word, “I Sara am”. Almost every Persian sentence ends with its verb, so the end is where to listen for what is happening.

blocks.means: a group of words that says something complete: I'm from Canada.
a word for doing or being: am, go, eat, want. In Persian it comes at the end of the sentence.
a short word that stands for a person or a thing: I, you, he, she.

blocks.p: **I and you.** {{من|man}} is “I”. For “you” there are two words: {{تو|to}} for a friend, a child or family, and {{شما|shomâ}} for anyone else, and for more than one person. When in doubt, say {{شما}}: it is polite and never wrong. The end of the verb follows the pronoun: -am for “I”, -i for {{تو}}, -id for {{شما}}.

table: to a friend, a child, family
to anyone else (polite), or to several people

blocks.p: **Where from?** {{اهل|ahl}} means “from”, for where a person belongs: {{اهل ایران هستم.|ahl-e irân hastam.}} “I'm from Iran.” The short -e after it in the reading is the **ezafe**, a little sound that joins words together. Persian doesn't write it; lesson 3 is all about it.

ex.note: no word for “a”: {{دانشجو|dâneshju}} is “student” or “a student”
a question just by raising your voice at the end
{{است|ast}} is “is”; word for word “name-of me Karim is”
said when you meet someone; word for word “I'm fortunate”

blocks.tip: Persian is written from right to left, and its short vowels (a, e, o) aren't written: {{من|man}} is just the letters m and n. The reading in Latin letters gives every vowel, and tapping an example lets you hear it. In the reading, â is the long a of “father”, a the short a of “cat”.
{{سلام|salâm}} is “hello” at any time of day, to anyone.

mistakes.why: The verb goes at the end: “I Sara am”.
With {{شما}} the verb ends in -id: {{هستید}}. ({{هستی}} goes with {{تو}}.)

practice.q: You're meeting your new teacher. “You” is…
practice.why: {{شما|shomâ}} is the polite “you”: use it with anyone you don't know well.

practice.q: Choose the missing word.
You're Sam, from England. Choose your replies.

lines.why: The verb {{هستم}} goes at the end.

practice.q: Put the words in order.
Ask someone politely: “Where are you from?”
Your turn: say hello, your name and where you're from. Start with {{سلام، من…}}

answers.t: سلام، من مایکل هستم. اهل آمریکا هستم.
answers.r: salâm, man mâykel hastam. ahl-e âmrikâ hastam.
answers.tr: Hello, I'm Michael. I'm from America.

answers.t: سلام، من ماریا هستم. اهل اسپانیا هستم.
answers.r: salâm, man mâriyâ hastam. ahl-e espâniyâ hastam.
answers.tr: Hello, I'm Maria. I'm from Spain.

lessons.title: Point at things and name them
lessons.summary: Ask “What's this?”, and say what something is and what it isn't.

goal.t: این چیست؟ این یک هدیه است.
goal.r: in chist? in yek hedye ast.

dialog.t: و آن چیست؟ آن هم چای است؟
dialog.r: va ân chist? ân ham chây ast?
dialog.tr: And what's that? Is that tea too?

dialog.t: نه، آن چای نیست. آن قهوه است.
dialog.r: na, ân chây nist. ân ghahve ast.
dialog.tr: No, that isn't tea. That's coffee.

blocks.p: **This and that.** {{این|in}} is “this”, for something near you; {{آن|ân}} is “that”, further away. The thing comes next, and {{است|ast}} “is” at the end: {{این چای است.|in chây ast.}} “This is tea.”

blocks.means: a word for a person, a place or a thing: tea, book, Tehran, friend.

blocks.p: **No “the”, and no “he” or “she” for things.** {{کتاب|ketâb}} is “book”, “a book” and “the book”: the situation tells you which. For “a” you can add {{یک|yek}} “one”: {{این یک کتاب است.|in yek ketâb ast.}} “This is a book.” And Persian has no masculine and feminine: nothing ever changes to agree with a word.
**What is it?** {{چه|che}} “what” and {{است}} join into one word, {{چیست|chist}} “what is”: {{این چیست؟|in chist?}} “What's this?”. The answer goes in its place: {{این چای است.}}

**Not.** “Isn't” is a word of its own, {{نیست|nist}}, in the place of {{است}}: {{این قهوه نیست.|in ghahve nist.}} “This isn't coffee.” “I'm not” is {{نیستم|nistam}}, with the same endings as {{هستم}}.

ex.note: {{کی|ki}} “who” + {{است}}: about a person in a photo, for example

blocks.tip: In everyday speech {{است}} often shrinks to a short -e: you'll hear {{این چیه؟|in chiye?}} for {{این چیست؟}}. This course writes the standard {{است}}, which is also what you see written.

mistakes.why: “Isn't” is one word, {{نیست}}, in the place of {{است}}.

practice.q: The cup you mean is far away, on another table. “That” is…
practice.why: {{آن|ân}} is “that”, further away; {{این|in}} is “this”, near you.

practice.q: Choose the missing word.
A friend is showing you around. Choose your replies.

lines.why: {{چیست}} already has “is” in it, and it goes at the end.
{{نیستم}} is “I'm not”: you'd be saying “I'm not a library!”

practice.q: Put the words in order.
Point at something and ask: “What's this?”
Your turn: name things around you, and say what one of them isn't. Use {{این … است}}, {{آن … است}} and {{نیست}}.

answers.t: این کتاب است. آن قهوه نیست، چای است.
answers.r: in ketâb ast. ân ghahve nist, chây ast.
answers.tr: This is a book. That isn't coffee, it's tea.

answers.t: این یک تلفن است و آن یک پنجره است.
answers.r: in yek telefon ast va ân yek panjere ast.
answers.tr: This is a phone and that's a window.

lessons.title: Describe people and things
lessons.summary: Say “a big city”, “the city is big” and “I'm tired”, with Persian's most important little sound: the ezafe.
lessons.topic: the ezafe (-e) between a noun and its adjective; adjective + {{است}}; the short “am, are”: {{خسته‌ام}}

dialog.t: بله، خیلی خوب است. یک خانهٔ کوچک ولی قشنگ است.
dialog.r: bale, kheyli khub ast. yek khâne-ye kuchak vali ghashang ast.
dialog.tr: Yes, it's very nice. It's a small but pretty house.

dialog.t: شهر بزرگ و شلوغ است، ولی خیلی زیباست.
dialog.r: shahr bozorg va sholugh ast, vali kheyli zibâst.
dialog.tr: The city is big and busy, but it's very beautiful.
I'm fine, but I'm very tired!

blocks.p: **Two ways to describe.** Compare {{شهر بزرگ است.|shahr bozorg ast.}} “The city is big.” with {{یک شهر بزرگ|yek shahr-e bozorg}} “a big city”. In the first, the describing word comes before {{است}} “is”, as in English. In the second, it comes **after** the noun, joined to it by a short **-e**: shahr-e bozorg, “city-of big”.

blocks.means: a word that describes a person or a thing: big, new, tired, Iranian.
the short -e (after a vowel, -ye) that joins a Persian noun to the word after it, the one that describes it or owns it: {{شهر بزرگ|shahr-e bozorg}} “a big city”. The word means “adding”.

blocks.p: **You hear the ezafe, but you usually don't see it.** After a consonant it isn't written at all: the reading shows it. After a vowel it becomes -ye and is written: as a small mark on a final {{ه}} ({{خانهٔ بزرگ|khâne-ye bozorg}} “a big house”) and as {{ی}} after {{ا}} or {{و}} ({{هوای خوب|havâ-ye khub}} “good weather”). More than one adjective? One more -e each time: {{یک ماشین قرمز قشنگ|yek mâshin-e ghermez-e ghashang}} “a pretty red car”.

table: a big city, the big city

blocks.p: **He or she.** {{او|u}} is both “he” and “she”: {{او خیلی مهربان است.|u kheyli mehrabân ast.}} is “He's very kind” or “She's very kind”.

blocks.means: a piece added to the end of a word that changes what it says: the -am of {{خسته‌ام|khaste-am}} “I'm tired”.

blocks.p: **I'm tired, you're well.** “Am” and “are” also have short forms: endings that hang on the describing word. {{خسته‌ام|khaste-am}} “I'm tired”, {{خوبی؟|khubi?}} “are you well?”. They are the endings of {{هستم}}, {{هستی}}… without the {{هست}}. For “he, she, it is”, keep {{است}}. After a final {{ه}} a small gap comes before the ending (the hyphen in the reading).

ex.tr: The new book is very good.

ex.note: word for word “the air is very cold”

blocks.tip: {{خیلی|kheyli}} “very” goes before the adjective, as in English: {{خیلی خوب|kheyli khub}} “very good”.

mistakes.why: The adjective comes after the noun, joined by -e: shahr-e bozorg.
Without {{است}} it is only “this good book”: a sentence needs its verb.

practice.q: Which one is a whole sentence: “The car is red”?
practice.why: With {{است}} it says something: “The car is red.” With the -e and no verb it is just “a red car”.

practice.q: Choose the missing word.
practice.why: “I am” is the ending -am: {{خسته‌ام}}. ({{خسته است}} is “he or she is tired”.)

practice.q: Your friend calls to ask about your new city. Choose your replies.

options: یک بزرگ و زیبا شهر است.
lines.why: Adjectives come after the noun: {{شهر بزرگ و زیبا}}.

practice.q: Put the words in order.
Order “a hot tea, please”.
Your turn: describe your town or your home in two sentences: one with an adjective after a noun ({{یک شهر کوچک}}), one with {{است}}.

answers.t: من اهل یک شهر کوچک هستم. هوا آنجا خیلی خوب است.
answers.r: man ahl-e yek shahr-e kuchak hastam. havâ ânjâ kheyli khub ast.
answers.tr: I'm from a small town. The weather there is very good.

answers.t: لندن یک شهر بزرگ و شلوغ است.

The house is small but pretty.

lessons.title: Say whose it is
lessons.summary: Say “my name”, “Sara's bag” and “your phone”, with the ezafe and the little endings for “my, your, his”.
lessons.topic: the ezafe with an owner: {{کیف سارا|kif-e sârâ}}; the possessive endings -am, -at, -ash, -emân, -etân, -eshân

goal.t: اسم من مریم است. اسم شما چیست؟
goal.r: esm-e man maryam ast. esm-e shomâ chist?
goal.tr: My name is Maryam. What's your name?

dialog.tr: Excuse me, is this your bag?

dialog.t: نه، کیفم آبی است. این کیف دوستم است.
dialog.r: na, kifam âbi ast. in kif-e dustam ast.
dialog.tr: No, my bag is blue. This is my friend's bag.

blocks.p: **Whose? The ezafe again.** The owner comes after the thing, joined by the same -e as an adjective: {{کیف سارا|kif-e sârâ}} “Sara's bag” (“bag-of Sara”), {{اسم من|esm-e man}} “my name” (“name-of me”), {{خانهٔ شما|khâne-ye shomâ}} “your house”.

blocks.means: a word or an ending that says whose something is: my, your, Sara's.

blocks.p: **Or a short ending.** “My”, “your”, “his” can also be endings on the thing: {{کیفم|kifam}} “my bag”, {{کیفت|kifat}} “your bag”, {{کیفش|kifash}} “his bag” or “her bag”. Both ways are right: {{اسم من}} and {{اسمم|esmam}} both mean “my name”. The endings are shorter, and everyday speech uses them most.

**A thing, its adjective and its owner:** the adjective first, then the owner, all joined with -e: {{کیف آبی من|kif-e âbi-ye man}} “my blue bag”; or with the ending on the last word: {{کیف آبی‌ام|kif-e âbi-am}}.

ex.note: to a friend; to anyone else, {{اسمتان چیست؟|esmetân chist?}}
the polite everyday greeting; word for word “how is your state?”

mistakes.why: The owner comes after the thing: “bag-of me”, kif-e man.
Either {{اسم من}} or {{اسمم}}, not both: the ending already says “my”.

practice.q: {{کتابش|ketâbash}} means…
practice.why: {{ـش|-ash}} is “his” or “her”: Persian doesn't say which.

practice.q: Choose the missing word.
practice.why: “Your”, politely, is {{شما}} after the ezafe: esm-e shomâ.

lines.tr: Excuse me, is this your phone?

lines.why: “My phone” is {{گوشی من}}: the owner after the thing. ({{من گوشی است}} says “I is a phone”!)

practice.q: Choose the missing word.

Your turn: introduce someone in your family or a friend: their name and one thing about them. Use {{اسمش…}} or {{اسم … من}}.

answers.t: این برادرم است. اسمش علی است.
answers.r: in barâdaram ast. esmash ali ast.
answers.tr: This is my brother. His name is Ali.

lessons.title: Ask questions
lessons.summary: Ask where, what, who, when, how and why, and ask yes-or-no questions, the Persian way.
lessons.topic: yes/no questions with the voice or {{آیا}}; question words in the answer's place: {{کجا}}, {{چه}}, {{کی}}, {{چند}}, {{چطور}}, {{چرا}}

goal.tr: Excuse me, where's the metro station?

dialog.t: من معلم هستم. شما اهل کجا هستید؟
dialog.r: man mo'allem hastam. shomâ ahl-e kojâ hastid?
dialog.tr: I'm a teacher. Where are you from?

blocks.p: **Yes-or-no questions.** Say the sentence and raise your voice at the end: {{شما دانشجو هستید؟|shomâ dâneshju hastid?}} “Are you a student?”. Nothing else changes. In writing, or to sound careful, you can begin with {{آیا|âyâ}}, a word that only says “here comes a question”: {{آیا شما دانشجو هستید؟}}

**Question words stay where the answer goes.** English moves “where” to the front; Persian leaves it in the answer's place. The answer: {{اهل لندن هستم.|ahl-e landan hastam.}} “I'm from London.” The question: {{اهل کجا هستید؟|ahl-e kojâ hastid?}}, “from where are you?”. Put the question word where the answer would be, and you have your question.

table: {{او کیست؟|u kist?}} Who's he? Who's she?
{{کلاس کی است؟|kelâs key ast?}} When's the class?
{{حالت چطور است؟|hâlat chetowr ast?}} How are you?
{{این چند است؟|in chand ast?}} How much is this?
{{چرا خسته‌ای؟|cherâ khaste-i?}} Why are you tired?

blocks.p: {{کی}} is two words written the same way: read **ki** it is “who”, read **key** it is “when”. The reading tells you, and so does the sentence.

**Short forms.** After a question word that ends in a vowel, {{است}} loses its first letter and joins on: {{کجا}} + {{است}} → {{کجاست|kojâst}} “where is”, {{چه}} + {{است}} → {{چیست|chist}} “what is”, {{کی}} + {{است}} → {{کیست|kist}} “who is”.

ex.note: {{آیا}} makes it a little more careful; it can be left out

blocks.tip: To answer: {{بله|bale}} “yes” ({{آره|âre}} with friends) and {{نه|na}} “no”. To start a question to a stranger, say {{ببخشید|bebakhshid}} “excuse me”.

mistakes.why: The question word goes where the answer would go: “you from where are?”.
The thing you're asking about comes first, then {{کجاست}} “where is”, at the end like every verb.

practice.q: Which question asks “When is the class?”
Choose the missing word.
Put the words in order.
Someone at a party asks you questions. Choose your replies.

lines.why: The answer goes where {{کجا}} was: {{اهل لندن هستم}}.

practice.q: Ask a friend: “Why are you tired?”
Your turn: write two questions you'd ask someone you've just met, each with a different question word.

answers.t: حالتان چطور است؟ چرا اینجا هستید؟
answers.r: hâletân chetowr ast? cherâ injâ hastid?

lessons.title: Say what you have
lessons.summary: Say what you have and don't have (a brother, a car, time, thirty years!), with the endings every Persian verb uses.
lessons.topic: {{داشتن}} “to have”: {{دارم}}… {{ندارم}}; the personal endings; leaving out “I” and “you”

goal.t: دو برادر دارم، ولی خواهر ندارم.
goal.r: do barâdar dâram, vali khâhar nadâram.
goal.tr: I have two brothers, but I don't have a sister.

dialog.tr: Excuse me, do you have water?
Yes, we do. Cold or not?
Cold, please. Do you have bread too?
No, I'm afraid we don't have bread.

blocks.p: **Have.** {{دارم|dâram}} “I have”, {{داری|dâri}} “you have”, {{دارد|dârad}} “he, she has”… The verb is at the end, as always: {{یک ماشین دارم.|yek mâshin dâram.}} “I have a car.”

**The endings say who.** Look at the ends: -am, -i, -ad, -im, -id, -and. They are the same on almost every Persian verb, in almost every tense, so learning them once pays off for good. And because the ending already says who, {{من}}, {{تو}}… are usually left out: {{دارم}} alone is “I have”. Say {{من دارم}} only to stress it: “**I** have”.

blocks.means: who or what does the action: “I” in “I have”. In Persian the verb's ending shows it, so the word itself is often left out.

blocks.p: **Not.** Put {{نـ|na-}} on the front of the verb: {{ندارم|nadâram}} “I don't have”. Almost every Persian verb is made negative this way.
**Age.** Persian “has” years: {{بیست سال دارم.|bist sâl dâram.}} “I'm twenty.” And {{چند سال دارید؟|chand sâl dârid?}} “How old are you?”

ex.note: to a friend; a question by the voice
word for word “I have thirty years”

ex.tr: Do you have a free room?

blocks.tip: Most Persian verbs have {{می|mi-}} in front in the present ({{می‌خواهم|mi-khâham}} “I want”, next lesson). {{دارم}} is one of the few that don't.

practice.q: Choose the missing word.
